Exxon and Chevron more than doubled year-ago profits, combining for $26.6 billion in Q2 as the Strait of Hormuz closure spiked crude prices. Gas prices surged from under $3 to $4.06 a gallon since the Iran war began, and Trump threatening to bomb mediator Oman risks driving them higher. Exxon and Chevron's integrated models capture profits from well to pump, but a Hormuz peace deal could collapse the windfall almost overnight. Oil has become one of the clearest financial beneficiaries of the Iran war -- and one of the biggest headaches for American drivers. The Strait of Hormuz, a critical artery for global energy shipments, remains effectively closed, with little tanker traffic moving through the waterway. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude is above $82 a barrel and Brent is above $88, compared with roughly $73 Brent before the war. The result has been a windfall for Big Oil. Bloomberg reported in July that combined earnings for the five supermajors were on track to be the third-highest in history, while several companies have already reported profits more than double a year ago. Exxon Mobil (NYSE:XOM) reported $14.5 billion of second-quarter profit, up from $7.1 billion a year earlier. Chevron (NYSE:CVX) reported $12.1 billion, compared with $3.1 billion. Together, they generated roughly $26.6 billion in quarterly earnings. Both companies are integrated -- meaning they produce crude, refine it into gasoline and diesel, and market those products. That matters when a geopolitical shock disrupts the entire energy chain. Chevron's upstream earnings jumped to $8.2 billion, while downstream earnings reached $4.9 billion. Exxon generated $17.2 billion of free cash flow and returned $9.4 billion to shareholders through dividends and buybacks. Their stocks reflect that strength, with Exxon and Chevron both up 33% year-to-date. Neither, though, is at its March peak, leaving room for further gains if crude prices remain elevated.                                 © 24/7 Wall St. Trump has repeatedly accused oil companies of gouging consumers, singling out Exxon, Chevron, BP (NYSE:BP), and Shell (NYSE:SHEL), and demanding lower prices. In June, he said gasoline should be $2.25 a gallon and ordered a Justice Department investigation into potential price gouging. However, Exxon and Chevron don't simply choose the price posted at every gas station. Local competition, regional supply, refining margins, transportation costs, and crude prices all influence what motorists pay. AAA's national average was about $4.06 a gallon this morning, versus $3.98 a month earlier and $3.11 a year ago. Gasoline had been below $3 before the Iran war began. Notably, widening the war could make Trump's price problem worse. Trump has repeatedly extended the truce to give negotiations with Iran more time. Yet Iran continues threatening shipping through Hormuz, and Reuters reported today that Tehran is considering a shift to a "fully offensive" posture if diplomacy fails. Now Trump has threatened to bomb Oman if it "gets in the way" of peace talks. Oman is a U.S. ally and has been mediating between Washington and Tehran. An attack on Oman would introduce another Middle Eastern country into the conflict. If other Gulf states that have so far remained outside the fighting begin choosing sides, the market could price an even larger supply disruption. That would be bullish for Exxon and Chevron's upstream businesses and potentially their refining operations. But investors shouldn't assume every additional $10 in crude translates directly into another $10 billion of profit. Demand can weaken, refining margins can reverse, and a peace deal reopening Hormuz could send oil prices sharply lower. Brent crude is already well below its $126 wartime peak. In short, Exxon and Chevron are unusually well positioned for a prolonged oil shock because their integrated businesses can capture profits from production through refining and marketing. Another escalation could push quarterly earnings above their already massive Q2 totals -- but investors shouldn't chase the stocks solely on the prospect of war. The better thesis is that Exxon and Chevron have demonstrated they can convert elevated crude and refining margins into billions of dollars of cash. If Hormuz remains closed, that cash machine could keep running. If peace finally reopens the strait, the windfall can disappear almost as quickly as it arrived. content: Exxon Mobil XOM, the integrated oil-and-gas giant, jumped approximately 1.9% to $167.93 Thursday morning as oil prices ripped higher and the Strait of Hormuz remained the market's biggest supply wildcard. Brent surged $2.19 to $93.81 per barrel, extending its rally to a fifth straight session. The setup is simple: fewer barrels moving freely through one of the world's most important energy chokepoints means higher crude prices, and higher crude prices put Exxon's upstream cash machine directly in the spotlight. Reuters has reported that vessel traffic through Hormuz remains severely constrained as the U.S.-Iran standoff continues. Exxon does not need much help when oil is already pushing toward $94. The company entered this rally after generating second-quarter operating cash flow of $23.6 billion, free cash flow of $17.2 billion and earnings of $14.5 billion. Now crude is moving higher again. That combination gives investors exactly what they want from an oil major: huge production, huge cash generation and direct exposure to stronger commodity pricing. But the stock is no longer cheap by the GF Value yardstick. At $167.93, Exxon sits 33.93% above its GF Value estimate of $125.39a sizable premium that shows how aggressively the market is already pricing the story. That 33.93% premium is the number investors should watch. Exxon can print more upstream profit if crude stays near these levels, but $90-plus oil comes with baggage: inflation can heat up, consumers can pull back and interest rates can stay restrictive. Exxon's refining and chemicals operations give it more protection than a pure-play producer, but the stock still carries a meaningful geopolitical premium. If Hormuz stays disrupted, Exxon's cash engine gets even more fuel. If shipping normalizes and oil retreats, a stock trading nearly 34% above GF Value suddenly has much less room for disappointment. title: Does Cenovus Have a Clear Path to Achieve Nearly 1.1 MMBoe/d by 2028? - The Globe and Mail
content: Cenovus Energy Inc. CVE is a Canadian integrated energy company with upstream operations in Canada and Asia-Pacific and downstream refining operations in Canada and the United States. In the second quarter of 2026, upstream production reached about 970,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (Boe/d), an increase of more than 200,000 Boe/d from the prior-year quarter. CVE raised its 2026 production guidance to 970,000-1.01 million barrels of oil equivalent per day (MMBoe/d) and is targeting nearly 1.1 MMBoe/d by the end of 2028, supported by growth investments with forward capital efficiency of less than $25,000 per flowing barrel. Achieving this target is underpinned by several projects that are either completed or currently in progress. Christina Lake North is expected to add about 40,000 barrels per day (bbl/d) by the end of 2028 through redevelopment wells, additional steam generation and debottlenecking. Sunrise optimization is expected to add 15,000-20,000 bbl/d from 2024 to 2028, while West White Rose is expected to achieve first oil in third-quarter 2026 and reach net peak production of about 45,000 bbl/d in 2028.Cenovus is already showing strong momentum, with second-quarter 2026 oil sands production reaching a record 786,000 Boe/d. Its growth portfolio also includes Narrows Lake, Foster Creek optimization and Spruce Lake DilSAP. CVE states that its growth projects remain economically viable at US$45 West Texas Intermediate ("WTI"), supported by oil sands operating and sustaining capital costs of about $21 per barrel. Together, the strong existing production base and visible project additions give Cenovus a clear path toward nearly 1.1 MMBoe/d by the end of 2028. Some other energy companies with a clearer near- to medium-term production growth path are Sunoco LP SUN and ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM. Sunoco operates across oil sands, upgrading, offshore production, refining, marketing and trading. The partnership plans to increase upstream production by about 100,000 bbl/d by 2028, supported by growth at its oil sands operations. During its second-quarter 2026 earnings call, Sunoco mentioned that its growth plan is largely within its control and supported by a large, high-quality resource base, particularly its in-situ assets. Management noted that preparatory work is underway and that SUN has flexibility to accelerate growth if market conditions support it. ExxonMobil is a well-known energy giant that operates in oil and gas production, refining, chemicals and low-carbon solutions. In its second-quarter 2026 results, the company highlighted record Permian production of more than 1.8 MMBoe/d, consistent with its planned 9% compound annual growth rate through 2030. XOM expects its fifth Guyana FPSO to begin production in the fourth quarter of 2026, adding 250,000 bbl/d of production capacity and providing another driver of future upstream growth. Cenovus shares have risen 118.6% over the past year compared with the industry’s 90% growth. From a valuation standpoint, CVE trades at a trailing 12-month enterprise-value-to-EBITDA (EV/EBITDA) of 5.96X. This is below the broader industry average of 6.19X. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for CVE's 2026 earnings has remained constant over the past seven days. CVE currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). Electricity infrastructure is becoming more significant as global power consumption expands. Exxon Mobil's exposure to natural gas and other energy infrastructure gives the company several possible connections to this changing landscape. Growing grid requirements could increase demand for reliable energy supplies capable of supporting power generation during periods of elevated consumption. This creates another area where the company's existing assets and project capabilities may become strategically relevant. The significance of grid exposure will ultimately depend on commercial agreements, project economics, and measurable operating contributions. Cash-flow visibility remains one of the clearest ways to assess whether Exxon Mobil's strategy is translating into durable business performance. Strong operating cash generation can provide flexibility for project development, balance-sheet management, and broader corporate priorities. Power demand, energy pricing, project execution, capital spending, and contract quality all feed into that outlook. Rather than viewing these themes separately, their combined effect provides a stronger framework for understanding the company's direction. Exxon Mobil's evolving story therefore rests on execution. Consistent operating evidence will remain essential as the company responds to changing energy demand while balancing growth ambitions with financial discipline. title: ExxonMobil’s Return Comes From Somewhere The Index Does Not Go - Trefis
content: A five-year correlation this low is not a statistical curiosity; it is what an earnings stream built on barrels and product margins looks like beside the index. ExxonMobil (XOM) has gained 4.3% over the last five trading days while the S&P 500 slipped 0.5%, and a stock rising while the tape sags is the kind that gets chased. But the question that decides your outcome is different: how much of this return is its own story rather than the index you already own, and what owning it does to your swings. On five years of evidence, most of that return is not the index. Most Of What Moves This Stock Is Not What Moves The Index Over the past five years ExxonMobil’s correlation to the S&P 500 has been 0.26, on a scale where 1.0 would mean lockstep. Gold, the asset investors hold precisely because it does its own thing, correlates to this stock at 0.1 over the same five years. The index reading is higher, and still describes a stock that has largely moved independently of the broad market. That independence has not cost return, though it has cost calm: the stock annualized 30.2% over that window against 13.2% for the index, at 26.7% volatility versus 17.2%. Barrels And Product Margins Are What Set This Return Stream That independence comes from what the company sells. In the second quarter of 2026 ExxonMobil lost roughly 10% of its upstream production to the Middle East conflict and still earned $14.5 billion. By its own account, its North American facilities met the supply shortfall that disruption created, driving a roughly 180% increase in chemical product margins versus the first quarter of 2026, while its Gulf Coast refining operations answered a tight diesel market with record second quarter diesel production. That is the operating reality behind a low correlation: earnings that answer to oil supply and product margins. The quarter threw off $23.6 billion of cash flow from operations. Cash generation of that kind is one of the properties the Trefis High Quality Portfolio looks for. Over The Past Year It Tended To Rise On The Market’s Down Days The capture readings, which measure the share of the index’s move the stock caught over a one-year window rather than five, show something stronger than independence. On days the S&P 500 fell over the past year, ExxonMobil moved about 110% in the opposite direction, tending to rise as the index dropped. On the market’s up days it moved about 32% of the index’s move in the opposite direction, tending to fall when the index rose. That is counter-cyclical rather than muted, and both halves are one trait: the cushion on a bad week is paid for by giving some back on the good ones. A one-year reading can shift. What Would Undo The Margin Support Is Capacity Coming Back The role it can play, then, is a return engine the index does not supply, bought at a wider swing. What would change it is what created it: management counts roughly 3 million barrels a day of capacity missing from the market, and expects a robust refining market with very high margins while that holds. Watch for that supply returning, because the margin support behind these earnings goes when it does. The swing is the price of the independence. A stock that moves on its own is still one company’s exposure to one commodity cycle, and that cushion is a byproduct, not a substitute for spreading risk. The Trefis High Quality Portfolio is built the other way around, spreading that risk across quality businesses. That portfolio has a track record of outpacing the three major indices – the S&P 500, S&P Mid-cap, and Russell 2000. ©Copyright 2026 Insight Guru Inc. All Rights Reserved. title: Targa Resources' Stock Near 52-Week High: Time to Lock in Gains? - The Globe and Mail
content: Shares of Targa Resources Corp.TRGP closed at $297.77 on Tuesday, near its 52-week high of $305.08, following a surge of 85.2% in a year. The stock price rally was followed by a positive long-term agreement with ExxonMobil Holdings CorporationXOM across the Permian.During the same time period, the company’s shares outperformed the sub-industry and the broader oil and energy sector’s rise of 51.6% and 37.6%, respectively. Peer comparison further highlights the strength, as Targa Resources conveniently outpaced its peers: Sunoco LPSUN and Western Midstream Partners, LPWES, which climbed 48.8% and 30.4%, respectively, in the past year. Targa Resources continues to benefit from strong demand for its Permian and Gulf Coast midstream network, enabling the company to convert this demand into steady and durable cash flows. Headquartered in Houston, TX, Targa Resources operates at the center of the U.S. midstream energy infrastructure and delivers essential services across the natural gas and natural gas liquids (NGL) value chain. Its operations include gathering, treating, compressing, processing, transporting and storing these resources. The company runs its business through two main segments — Gathering & Processing and Logistics & Transportation. A significant portion of Targa Resources’ revenues comes from fee-based contracts, which help provide a relatively stable income stream even during periods of commodity price volatility. That said, investors are now weighing whether TRGP’s strong rally still has room to continue or if much of its future growth is already priced into the stock. With solid momentum and an encouraging outlook, the company’s prospects merit a closer look before deciding whether to buy, hold or lock in profits. Long-Term Growth Visibility From ExxonMobil Agreements: Targa Resources’ new 20-year agreements with ExxonMobil provide strong long-term volume visibility and reinforce its growth outlook. The contracts add significant acreage dedications across the Permian Delaware and Midland basins, covering gathering, processing, treating, NGL transportation and fractionation through 2046. The agreements are expected to drive substantial volume growth across TRGP’s integrated infrastructure and support growth well into the next decade. New processing plants and the Bull Run II pipeline further position the company to capture rising Permian production, supporting durable and growing adjusted free cash flow. A Positive 2026 Earnings Estimate: The Zacks Consensus Estimate for TRGP’s 2026 earnings is pegged at $11.01 per share, indicating 29.7% year-over-year growth. Additionally, the consensus mark for 2026 revenues is pegged at $19.12 billion, also implying a 12.3% year-over-year rise. The positive earnings estimate outlook makes the stock attractive for investors. In comparison to Targa Resources, the Zacks Consensus Estimate of the above-mentioned peer companies, namely Sunoco and Western Midstream, also indicates positive year-over-year growth for 2026. Strong Permian Volume Growth Supports Long-Term Earnings: Targa Resources is benefiting from robust producer activity across the Permian Basin, with second-quarter volumes reaching a record 7.2 Bcf/d, up 7% sequentially and 14% year over year. Despite 200-400 MMcf/d of gas being shut in during the quarter because of weak Waha prices, volumes still increased by 450 MMcf/d from the first quarter. Most price-related curtailments returned in July, while producer activity remains strong. Targa Resources expects continued volume growth through the second half of 2026 and into 2027, supported by improving gas prices and better takeaway capacity. This growing throughput should support its gathering, processing and downstream businesses. Major Growth Projects Could Drive Significant Future EBITDA: Targa Resources has a substantial portfolio of organic projects that should expand its processing, transportation, fractionation and export capacity. Five Permian processing plants — Copperhead I and II, Yeti I and II, and Roadrunner III — are on track, while East Driver has already started operations ahead of schedule. Train 11 is online and highly utilized, with Trains 12 and 13 progressing. Speedway and the LPG export expansion are expected in the third quarter of 2027 and should provide meaningful operating leverage. Management expects these investments to support a strong EBITDA and free-cash-flow inflection over time. High Growth Capital Spending Could Pressure Free Cash Flow: Targa Resources' growth opportunity requires substantial capital investment, which could constrain free cash flow and shareholder returns in the near term. The company expects approximately $4.5 billion of net growth capital spending in 2026, compared with only $250 million of maintenance capital. Although these investments are designed to generate high returns and support future EBITDA growth, the scale of spending means the company remains heavily dependent on successful project execution and continued volume growth. Management itself expects the more meaningful free-cash-flow inflection to occur only after major projects such as Speedway and the LPG export expansion come online in the third quarter of 2027. Marketing Gains Are Likely to Moderate: A significant portion of TRGP's exceptional first-half performance came from market optimization opportunities that were not incorporated into its original guidance. Management indicated that the first half benefited from approximately $250 million of optimization margin, but expects materially lower marketing opportunities in the second half as basis spreads narrow and Waha gas prices improve. Management specifically acknowledged that the third quarter will face a headwind from weaker marketing benefits compared with the second quarter. Therefore, investors should not assume that the unusually strong marketing contribution seen earlier in 2026 will continue at the same level. Commodity Prices Still Create Some Earnings Exposure: Although Targa Resources has increasingly shifted its G&P contracts toward fee-based structures, part of its portfolio remains commodity-sensitive. Management noted that commodity prices were a slight headwind to G&P results during the second quarter, while the company also remains below aggregate fee-floor levels across its portfolio. A sustained improvement in gas and NGL prices could eventually provide a tailwind, but near-term earnings remain exposed to commodity-price movements and the balance between gas, NGL and crude economics. This creates some uncertainty around per-unit margins even when physical volumes continue to grow strongly. TRGP’s Premium Valuation: From a valuation perspective — in terms of Enterprise Value to Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization (EV/EBITDA) ratio — Targa Resources is trading at a premium of 15.24 compared with the industry average of 12.35. The stock is also trading above its five-year mean of 12.02. Targa Resources remains a compelling midstream growth story, supported by its 20-year agreements with ExxonMobil, which provide strong long-term volume visibility along with strong stock performance as compared to peers like SUN and WES, while record Permian volumes and robust producer activity also support sustained growth. A substantial pipeline of processing, fractionation and export projects, along with positive 2026 earnings and revenue estimates, should strengthen EBITDA and free cash flow over time. However, these opportunities come with meaningful risks. TRGP’s approximately $4.5 billion of 2026 growth capital spending could constrain near-term free cash flow and make returns dependent on successful project execution. In addition, marketing gains are expected to moderate, while commodity-price exposure could create earnings volatility. The stock also trades at a premium valuation against its industry average. Given the company's attractive long-term growth prospects but limited margin for error at current valuation levels, retaining this Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) company appears prudent. Existing investors can benefit from future growth execution, while new investors may prefer to wait for a more attractive entry point or greater visibility on project returns and volume growth. title: Cenovus Energy is Undervalued: Should You Bet on the Stock Now? - The Globe and Mail
content: Cenovus Energy Inc. CVE is currently considered undervalued on a relative basis, with the stock trading at 5.97x trailing 12-month Enterprise Value to Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization (EV/EBITDA), which is a discount compared with the broader industry average of 6.11x. ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM and Chevron CVX, two other integrated energy majors, are valued at 9.24x and 7.76x, respectively. Such a discounted valuation often signals an entry point. However, before making investment decisions, one should consider the company's overall business environment and fundamentals. West Texas Intermediate (“WTI”) is currently trading above $85 per barrel, according to data from Oilprice.com, significantly higher than the shut-in and breakeven prices for existing wells in key resources. The escalation of conflicts in the Middle East has been aiding the rally in commodity prices. In its latest short-term energy outlook, the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) projects the WTI spot price to average $80.88 per barrel this year, a level that should remain supportive of upstream operations.  As a result, CVE’s upstream operations are benefiting from higher benchmark oil prices, which are eventually increasing oil sands production. High oil prices are also benefiting other energy majors like XOM and CVX. Image Source: The U.S. Energy Information Administration On the second-quarter 2026 earnings call, management noted that CVE’s refining business remained strong, with Canadian and U.S. refinery utilization at about 94% and 96%, respectively, supported by strong operational availability and favorable refined-product pricing. Also, since it has exposure to Canadian heavy oil, which is cheaper than lighter crude, CVE is likely to be enjoying a feedstock cost advantage. In other words, the company’s Canadian refining business is capable of using lower-priced fuel to produce high-value end products, giving it an edge over other refiners and helping it continue its upward trajectory. Investors’ strong preference for the stock is getting reflected in the price chart. In the past year, CVE has jumped 117.1%, outperforming the industry’s 86.1% growth. XOM and CVX have surged 52.6% and 34.3%, respectively, over the same time frame. Investors should also know that Cenovus expects higher spending in the second half because of major refinery maintenance, while some large tax payments are due mainly in early 2027. It also relies heavily on outside condensate supplies and still faces uncertainty around Canada’s carbon-tax rules. Hence, investors shouldn’t rush to buy the stock.  moved into sharper midweek focus on Wednesday as attention across the energy complex settled on the companys expanding output in Guyana and its widening footprint across the Permian Basin, two engines that continue to anchor cash generation among the integrated majors. The pairing of prolific offshore volumes with dense onshore acreage has become the defining feature of how the company is being described this week, and it frames the way market watchers are talking about the wider group of large diversified energy names. The story is less about any single headline number and more about the shape of the business. An integrated major carries barrels from the wellhead through refining and into chemicals, and ExxonMobil sits among the most recognizable examples of that structure. As the trading week reached its middle, the conversation around the stock leaned on how those layers fit together and how they might steady the company through the swings that define crude and natural gas. Guyana has become one of the most talked-about upstream regions in the world, and ExxonMobil operates at the heart of it. The offshore development in the Stabroek block has moved from exploration into a phase where new production vessels come online in sequence, each adding capacity to lift crude from deep water far off the coast. The appeal is straightforward in qualitative terms: the barrels tend to carry attractive per-unit economics, and the resource base has kept expanding as drilling confirms fresh discoveries. What makes the Guyana ramp-up notable this week is the cadence. Rather than a single burst of volume, the region is being brought forward in measured stages, with floating production units arriving one after another. That rhythm gives the company a runway of growing output without forcing a scramble, and it lets the operator refine its methods as each phase teaches something about the reservoir. For a company built around long-cycle projects, that steady progression is a familiar and comfortable pattern. If Guyana represents the offshore side of the growth narrative, the Permian Basin represents the onshore counterweight. Stretching across West Texas and southeastern New Mexico, the Permian remains the busiest oil-producing region in the country, and ExxonMobil has built a commanding position there. The addition of large adjacent acreage in recent times expanded the companys inventory of drilling locations and gave it more contiguous ground to work, which tends to lower the cost of moving equipment and laying gathering lines. Shale wells behave differently from deepwater projects. They come online quickly, decline quickly, and reward operators who can drill and complete at scale with tight cost control. ExxonMobil has leaned into that model, applying longer laterals and data-driven completion designs to squeeze more out of each section. The result is a Permian machine that can be dialed up or throttled back with more flexibility than the multi-year offshore developments, giving the company a useful lever as market conditions shift. The reason Guyana and the Permian keep coming up together is that both feed the same priority: durable cash generation. A business that spins off cash across the commodity cycle can fund its drilling program, sustain its dividend, and reduce debt without leaning too heavily on borrowing. That is the frame in which ExxonMobil is most often discussed, and it is why the pairing of low-cost offshore barrels with scalable onshore volumes draws so much notice. Cash generation also underwrites the companys habit of acquiring back stock over time. Dividends and buybacks together form the way large energy names distribute cash to the owners of their equity, and a company with two growing, low-cost supply sources is generally seen as better placed to keep that machinery running. None of this removes the sway of crude prices, but it does change the conversation from pure price-watching toward how efficiently the barrels are produced. An integrated major is more than an upstream driller. ExxonMobil refines crude into fuels, manufactures chemicals and specialty products, and markets those goods around the world. When crude prices climb, the upstream side tends to shine; when they fall, the downstream and chemicals arms can cushion the blow because their input costs ease. That natural hedge is the classic argument for the integrated structure, and it is a big part of why these companies are treated as core positions across the energy space. The chemicals arm, in particular, ties the company to broader industrial demand for plastics, packaging, and performance materials. It is a longer-cycle business that can smooth the sharper edges of commodity swings. Woven together, the upstream growth from Guyana and the Permian, the steadiness of refining, and the diversification of chemicals give ExxonMobil a spread of exposures that few pure-play drillers can match. The broader oil and gas backdrop is a study in cross-currents. Global demand for crude and refined fuels remains substantial, while the world simultaneously pushes toward cleaner sources of energy. That tension keeps the sector lively, and it shapes how capital is directed. Market watchers and operators alike track the balance between supply discipline among major producers and the pace of demand growth across transport, industry, and power generation. For anyone following oil and gas stocks, the way large majors navigate that balance is a recurring theme. ExxonMobils answer has leaned toward advantaged barrels, the low-cost, high-margin volumes that stay resilient even when prices soften. Guyana fits that description cleanly, and the best parts of the Permian do as well. The company has also placed bets on lower-carbon lines such as carbon capture and hydrogen, signaling that it intends to remain relevant as the energy mix evolves without abandoning the core that generates its cash today. Crude and natural gas prices have swung through wide ranges over recent seasons, driven by shifting supply decisions among major exporting nations, changing demand patterns, and the ripple effects of geopolitics. Natural gas has taken on added weight as liquefied exports connect once-regional markets into a more global web. For an integrated producer, this environment rewards flexibility and punishes overextension, and ExxonMobils mix of short-cycle shale and long-cycle offshore gives it options in both directions. The midweek tone around the stock reflects that reality. Rather than fixating on a single price print, the discussion has centered on how the company positions its volumes and how resilient its cash generation looks if prices wobble. That is a more durable way to frame an energy major, and it is consistent with how the largest names in the group are generally assessed. Within the peer set of global integrated majors, ExxonMobil is frequently described as one of the scale leaders, with a sprawling upstream portfolio, a heavy refining network, and a sizable chemicals arm. Its rivals pursue their own blends of offshore, onshore, and downstream exposure, and each has staked out a distinct path through the energy transition. As a component of the S&P 500, the company is a fixture in broad market-tracking portfolios, which keeps it in view even for those who do not follow energy closely. The competitive landscape is defined less by head-to-head rivalry over single assets and more by who can generate the most durable cash per barrel while keeping the balance sheet sturdy. On that measure, the combination of Guyanas economics and the Permians scale is exactly what keeps ExxonMobil near the front of the conversation among diversified producers. The developments drawing attention this week are cumulative rather than sudden. Each new production vessel offshore Guyana, each fresh batch of Permian wells, and each incremental step in cost efficiency adds to the narrative of growing, advantaged output. The company has also continued to talk up its longer-cycle projects and its lower-carbon ventures, framing itself as an operator that can grow supply today while preparing for a changing energy world. For observers, the takeaway is that the machine keeps advancing on multiple fronts at once. That breadth is part of why the stock stays in the midweek spotlight: there is rarely a moment when nothing is moving across such a large and varied portfolio. A recurring theme in how ExxonMobil is described is discipline. The company has spent recent seasons emphasizing structural cost reductions, tighter capital allocation, and a focus on the highest-margin barrels. In shale, that means drilling faster and completing smarter; offshore, it means standardizing designs so each new project builds on the last. The intent is to lower the break-even level at which the portfolio still generates healthy cash, which matters most when prices turn against producers. That operational focus is not glamorous, but it is central to the story. In a commodity business, the operators who survive downturns and thrive in upswings are usually the ones who kept their costs lean when times were good. ExxonMobils messaging has leaned hard into that idea, and it colors how the company is talked about even on quieter news days. That discipline shows up in the cadence of spending as well. By keeping its capital program steady and resisting the urge to chase every price spike, the company aims to smooth its path through the cycle so the drilling program and the distribution machinery can keep moving without sharp reversals. The advantaged nature of the Guyana and Permian barrels reinforces that steadiness, since low-cost volumes remain workable even when prices dip. It is a quiet kind of resilience, and it tends to matter most exactly when the sector turns turbulent and weaker operators are forced to retreat. The path is not without obstacles. The energy transition raises long-running questions about how demand for crude will evolve over the coming decades, and regulatory pressure around emissions continues to build in many regions. Price volatility remains a permanent feature of the business, and large projects always carry execution challenges, from weather offshore to supply-chain strains onshore. These are the headwinds every major must navigate, and ExxonMobil is no exception. The companys response has been to concentrate on advantaged resources and cost resilience while placing measured bets on lower-carbon technologies. That approach does not eliminate the challenges, but it aims to make the business more adaptable to whatever the period ahead brings. Because of its size and its place in widely tracked benchmarks, ExxonMobil functions as something of a bellwether for the energy sector. Moves in the stock ripple into how the broader group is perceived, and its commentary on demand, supply, and project timing is watched well beyond its own share register. As a large member of the S&P 500, the company carries weight in index-tracking portfolios and in the way the market reads the health of traditional energy. The midweek focus on Guyana and the Permian, then, is about more than one company. It is a window into how the largest integrated producers are trying to grow durable, low-cost supply while the world debates the shape of its energy mix. ExxonMobils blend of deepwater and shale, wrapped inside an integrated structure, keeps it central to that ongoing story. An upstream portfolio is only as durable as the reserves standing behind it, and ExxonMobil has framed much of its recent commentary around the depth of its resource base. Booked barrels in Guyana keep expanding as the drill bit confirms fresh accumulations, while the dense acreage across the Permian carries a long inventory of locations that can be developed for many seasons. That combination of proven volumes and probable additions gives the company a runway that stretches well beyond any single trading period. Replacing produced barrels with new ones is the quiet arithmetic that keeps a producer alive across the decades, and the pairing of offshore discoveries with onshore inventory is exactly the kind of balance that keeps reserve life healthy. It is a slow-moving measure, rarely the subject of daily headlines, yet it underpins the confidence with which the company describes the many seasons of drilling that lie in front of it. The downstream half of the business rarely grabs headlines the way a new offshore vessel does, yet it carries real weight in how the company is understood. Refineries convert crude into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and feedstocks, and the margins earned on that processing move on a rhythm of their own, sometimes strengthening exactly when raw crude softens. The chemicals arm reaches further still, turning hydrocarbons into the plastics, packaging, and performance materials that flow into countless industrial supply chains. Because these operations consume the very commodity the upstream side offers, they form an internal counterweight that steadies the combined earnings base. Manufacturing and logistics networks spread across continents let the company move product toward wherever demand runs strongest, capturing value at several links of the chain rather than a single one. That breadth of processing and marketing is a defining trait of the integrated model, and it widens the base from which cash is generated. The march toward a lower-carbon energy mix sits over every large producer, and ExxonMobil has answered it by pairing its traditional barrels with measured steps into carbon capture, hydrogen, and lower-emission fuels. Rather than abandoning the core that generates its cash, the company frames these ventures as extensions of the engineering and project skills it already owns, aiming to lower the emissions intensity of its operations while staying relevant as the mix evolves. Regulatory pressure around flaring, methane, and reported emissions continues to build across many regions, and operators that treat those expectations as design constraints rather than afterthoughts tend to face fewer surprises. The energy transition is best read as a long arc rather than a sudden turn, and a company that can supply advantaged barrels today while preparing for a cleaner tomorrow is trying to keep a foot in both worlds. That balancing act frames much of how the name is discussed across the sector.  drew fresh attention midweek as energy names across the US market pushed toward record territory, standing out on a session when the broader tape turned softer. The move traced back to a tightening crude market, where escalating Middle East tension and a tense standoff around the Strait of Hormuz have reshaped how traders think about the flow of barrels. As one of the largest integrated energy companies in the world, ExxonMobil sits close to the center of that story, and its shares reflected the shift in sentiment as customers rotated toward producers with heavy exposure to oil and natural gas. The backdrop this week has been unusual. While much of the market drifted, the energy complex firmed, drawing strength from a crude benchmark that has climbed as shipping lanes came into question. The Strait of Hormuz, a narrow channel through which a large share of seaborne crude typically passes, has become the focal point of the current tension, and any hint of disruption there ripples quickly through global pricing. For a company with ExxonMobils scale, that dynamic tends to lift the value of every barrel it lifts. The company moves its production into a global market, so a firmer benchmark reaches across its entire producing base rather than a single region. Traders watching the tape midweek treated that reach as a reason to lean toward the largest producers, and ExxonMobil sits at the front of that queue by sheer size. Crude does not trade in isolation from geopolitics, and the current episode makes that point plainly. Reports of tankers rerouting, of proposed bypass corridors, and of vessels avoiding the chokepoint have kept a firm bid under the benchmark. When the market perceives that supply could tighten, the price of oil tends to rise even before any physical shortfall appears, because customers move early to secure barrels. That anticipatory behavior has been on display this week, and it has fed directly into the tone across energy equities. For ExxonMobil, the mechanism is straightforward. The company produces crude and natural gas around the world, and higher benchmark pricing lifts the realized value of that output. At the same time, a tighter market tends to widen the spreads that refiners capture when they turn crude into fuels, a dynamic that touches the downstream side of the business. The combination is why an integrated major often behaves as a barometer for the entire complex when tension flares. Because ExxonMobil touches nearly every stage of the value chain, its shares tend to absorb signals from both crude and fuels at once, giving the market a single, closely watched reference point for how the whole sector is faring. That role as a bellwether has been on clear display through the current stretch of firm pricing. ExxonMobil operates across the full energy chain. Its upstream arm explores for and produces crude oil and natural gas across a wide geographic footprint, spanning onshore basins, deepwater developments, and liquefied natural gas ventures. Its downstream arm refines crude into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and other products, while its chemical business converts hydrocarbons into the building blocks used across manufacturing. That breadth is central to how the company weathers swings in any single link of the chain. The integrated structure gives the company a degree of balance. When crude prices climb, the upstream side captures the upside. When margins on fuels widen, the refining side benefits. And when petrochemical demand firms, the chemical segment adds another stream. This week, with crude firm and the sector strong, the parts of the business tied most directly to oil pricing have been the ones drawing the spotlight. Reinforcing the tone around the stock, ExxonMobil reported very strong results in its most recent quarter. The company generated robust cash from its operations, supported by firm commodity pricing and steady volumes across its core producing regions. Management has spent recent years reshaping the portfolio toward lower-cost, higher-yielding barrels, and the most recent period showed that work translating into strong headline figures. The refining side of the business contributed as well, with the company processing crude into fuels at a time when demand for transportation products stayed firm. Chemical operations added their own contribution, rounding out a quarter in which each major segment played a part. The strength of the report gave the market a fundamental anchor to pair with the geopolitical story, and the two together framed much of the midweek move. The downstream business deserves a closer look because it often gets overshadowed by the drama of crude prices. Refining margins depend on the gap between the cost of crude feedstock and the price of finished fuels, and that gap can widen sharply when supply concerns collide with steady demand. ExxonMobil operates a large, globally distributed refining network, and that scale lets it capture value across many markets at once. During periods of tension like the current one, the downstream arm can act as a stabilizer. Even as crude costs rise, strong demand for gasoline and diesel can keep the finished-product side healthy. That balance is part of why integrated majors tend to stay resilient when the energy complex firms, and it helps explain the resilience ExxonMobil has shown this week relative to the softer broad market. On the upstream side, ExxonMobil has concentrated its efforts on a handful of high-quality regions. Its position in the Permian basin of the US anchors its onshore output, delivering barrels at a cost structure the company has worked hard to lower. Offshore, its developments in Guyana have become a signature growth engine, ramping crude output from a series of deepwater projects that rank among the most closely watched in the industry. Liquefied natural gas ventures add a further dimension, connecting the company to markets far from its producing basins. Together, these engines give ExxonMobil a base of output that it can grow while keeping spending disciplined. In a week when crude pricing is firm, the value of that output rises, and the market has taken notice. Each of these regions carries a distinct cost profile, and the blend of onshore shale, deepwater crude, and liquefied gas gives the company a spread of exposures that few peers can match. That diversity of supply sources helps smooth the swings that come with any one basin, and it lets the company keep growing output while spending stays measured. The wider market has been mixed this week, with the S&P 500 drifting as attention rotated across sectors. Against that softer backdrop, energy stood out, and ExxonMobils move reflected the divergence. When the broad tape cools while one sector firms, it often signals that a specific theme is capturing capital, and the current crude tightening is exactly that kind of theme. Rotation of this sort is a familiar feature of energy markets. When geopolitics push crude higher, capital tends to flow toward the companies most levered to oil pricing, and the majors sit near the top of that list. ExxonMobil, as one of the most prominent names in the group, naturally draws attention when the rotation gathers pace. The broad basket of energy stocks has firmed as crude tightened, and the groups move toward record territory has been one of the defining features of the week. Within that basket, the integrated majors carry outsized weight because of their scale, and ExxonMobil ranks among the heaviest. When the sector runs, a company of its size tends to run with it, and the current stretch has been no exception. Sector strength of this kind reflects more than a single headline. It draws on the sense that firm crude pricing supports the entire chain, from wellhead to refinery gate. That breadth is why energy has been able to press higher even as other corners of the market lost momentum midweek. The sectors move toward records has been broad rather than narrow, reaching producers, refiners, and the service names that support them. When a rally stretches across so many corners of a single group at once, it tends to reflect a shared read on the direction of crude, and that shared read has kept the group firm through the week. Within the group of integrated majors, ExxonMobil occupies a distinctive place. Its combination of scale, geographic reach, and integration across the value chain gives it a broad base from which to operate. The company has spent recent years trimming costs, concentrating capital on its strongest assets, and streamlining its structure, and that work has sharpened how it competes against its peers. That positioning matters most when the market turns its focus to fundamentals. A company with low-cost barrels and a disciplined spending approach tends to generate strong cash across a range of price environments. When crude firms on top of that base, the effect compounds, and the strength shows up in results like those reported in the most recent quarter. Beyond the immediate crude story, several threads have shaped the picture around ExxonMobil. The continued ramp of its Guyana developments remains a central storyline, as each new phase adds barrels at attractive cost. Its Permian program continues to deliver steady onshore output, and its liquefied natural gas ventures keep expanding the companys reach into global gas markets. Each of these threads feeds the same narrative of disciplined growth. The company has also pressed forward with efforts to lower emissions intensity and to build out lower-carbon business lines, areas that have grown in importance across the industry. While crude pricing dominates the headlines this week, these longer-running initiatives form part of how the company frames its direction, and they add context to the broader story around the stock. A recurring theme in ExxonMobils approach has been discipline. Rather than chasing volume at any cost, the company has emphasized capital efficiency, directing spending toward the projects that deliver the strongest economics. That discipline shows up in a cost structure that has come down over recent years, allowing the company to generate strong cash even when crude is not at extreme levels. When crude firms, as it has this week, that discipline amplifies the effect. Lower costs mean more of each incremental dollar of revenue flows through to cash generation. The most recent quarter offered a clear illustration, with strong results built on a foundation of disciplined operations rather than on price alone. The industry is not without its complications. Crude pricing is inherently volatile, and the same geopolitical tension lifting prices this week could reverse if the standoff eases. Regulatory pressures, shifting demand patterns, and the long transition toward lower-carbon energy all shape how the majors plan. ExxonMobil, like its peers, must navigate these currents while keeping its core business healthy. Supply-chain constraints, cost inflation in certain services, and the challenge of replacing produced reserves add further complexity. These are the persistent features of the energy business, and they temper any simple reading of a strong week. Still, the companys scale and discipline give it a broad base from which to manage these challenges. The strength in ExxonMobil and its peers carries meaning beyond the sector itself. Energy prices feed into inflation, into consumer spending, and into the calculations that shape the broad market. When crude firms sharply, the effects ripple outward, touching everything from transportation costs to the tone of the wider tape. That is part of why a crude-driven rally in energy names draws attention well beyond the group. For the market as a whole, the current episode is a reminder of how quickly geopolitics can reshape sentiment. A standoff around a single waterway has firmed crude, lifted the energy complex, and pushed a name like ExxonMobil into the spotlight. As the week unfolds, the interplay between the geopolitical story and the fundamental strength shown in the most recent quarter will continue to frame how the market reads the stock. First and foremost, it's a fairly stable investment, as the company's dominant position in the industry ensures that it may not only succeed under adverse market conditions but also thrive when oil prices are high, as they are now. This is a top health insurance company in the country, and thus, demand for its services is likely to remain high for the foreseeable future. Healthcare is a necessity consumers can't do without, and UnitedHealth can grow due to population growth and rising rates. It's a behemoth in the industry, raking in $450 billion in revenue over the past year. While it may not be healthcare, these days, mobile phones and internet access are necessities for customers, so it will also generate a fairly consistent stream of income. Verizon generates just modest single-digit growth, but its business is rock-solid and fairly stable. With a payout ratio of around 70%, it also has plenty of room to continue raising its dividend, as it has in the past. Verizon has boosted its payout for an impressive 20 consecutive years. At 5.9%, it's easily the highest yield on this list, and with more dividend increases likely to come in the future, this makes for another terrific stock to buy right now. Shares of Verizon are up 18% this year, but they still look fairly undervalued, trading at less than 10 times the company's expected future earnings (based on analyst estimates). content: U.S. stock indices gained on Friday to end the week higher amid renewed hopes of diplomacy between the U.S. and Iran, while SpaceX’s strong trading debut fueled enthusiasm. The S&P 500 gained 0.5%, Nasdaq jumped 0.6% and the Dow Jones rose 0.7%. The Russell 2000, which tracks stocks with small market capitalizations, rallied 0.8%. Among sectors, materials and financials led gains, followed by technology and consumer stocks. Among ETFs tracking benchmark indexes, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) rose 0.6%, and Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) ended Friday around 0.7% higher, while the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) ended 0.7% higher. However, retail sentiment on Stocktwits for SPY, DIA and QQQ was ‘bearish’ as retail investors were still skeptical about the longevity of the ceasefire and expressed their lack of trust on the deal. One user highlighted skepticism on a peace deal between the U.S. and Iran. Trump grouses about 'weak and pathetic' Iran, dismisses 'leaked' deal Elon Musk’s SpaceX debuted on the Nasdaq at $150 per share, above its $135 IPO price, trading under the symbol SPCX. The stock closed up 19% at around $161. Elon Musk holds around 40% of the total equity in SpaceX, but due to different share classes with enhanced voting rights, his actual control over the firm reaches around 85%. In addition to the IPO frenzy, positive developments around the U.S.-Iran war also helped support broader equities and led oil prices lower. But, positive commentary from Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif helped push risk sentiment. The “final, agreed upon text” of a deal “has been reached,” Sharif said. Islamabad acted as a mediator between the U.S. and Iran. Furthermore, Bloomberg reported that a peace deal could be signed in Switzerland as soon as Sunday, citing people familiar with the plans. Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. Shares of Dianthus Therapeutics, Inc. (DNTH) jumped 8% on Friday after the company reported positive early data from its ongoing late-stage trial of claseprubart, an experimental drug for chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP). The DNTH stock, on Friday, clocked its best session since early March. CIDP is a rare nerve disorder that causes weakness, numbness and loss of function in the arms and legs. It occurs when the immune system mistakenly attacks the nerves. Current treatments often involve frequent infusions or steroids. In the first part of the study, 75% of the initial group of patients showed meaningful improvement after receiving claseprubart, Dianthus said. The company was expecting 50%, and the results clearly exceeded its own targets. The trial has a two-part design. In the initial part, patients received claseprubart. Those who improved were then moved into the next part of the study, where some continued on the drug, and others switched to a placebo. The goal is to see how long it takes for symptoms to return when the drug is stopped. The high response rate in the first part was seen across several measures of how well patients could move and function, the company said. Claseprubart is given as an under-the-skin injection every two weeks using a pre-filled pen, which could make it more convenient than current CIDP treatments like IVIG infusions. Dianthus also said on Friday that it now expects to provide guidance on the timing of the Part B top-line results by the end of 2026. Following the update, investment bank Raymond James reaffirmed its ‘Strong Buy’ rating on Dianthus and kept its price target at $125 per share. The analyst noted that the 75% response rate beat their expectations and stood out favorably compared to Sanofi’s competing drug. They also highlighted that the study’s design — starting with open treatment and then testing what happens when the drug is withdrawn — appears to be a lower-risk approach than the one used in Sanofi’s failed study. Sanofi discontinued its late-stage study of riliprubart in patients with CIDP who had failed or responded inadequately to standard treatments earlier this month. The company announced that an independent data monitoring committee had reviewed interim data and concluded the study was unlikely to meet its efficacy goals. The decision came after riliprubart had shown more modest results in an earlier mid-stage study, where roughly 50% of refractory patients improved at week 24. Sanofi is now evaluating whether to continue its other ongoing late-stage trial in patients already on maintenance IVIg. Dianthus, meanwhile, is also studying claseprubart in generalized myasthenia gravis and multifocal motor neuropathy as well. Microsoft is reportedly exploring ways to transform its gaming division, Xbox, into a wholly owned subsidiary, a joint venture or an entirely spun-out brand under the leadership of newly appointed gaming division CEO Asha Sharma. The structural considerations surface amid an aggressive internal turnaround plan spearheaded by Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, who took the helm in February, according to a report in The Information. Microsoft Chief Executive Satya Nadella and Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood have not ruled out a future structural split if it ultimately improves business operations or makes the division easier to sell. While three people with direct knowledge of the discussions told The Information that no restructuring plans are imminent, high-level discussions remain active. Shares of MSFT closed flattish, up 0.1% at Friday’s close. In an internal memo shared publicly, Sharma revealed that Xbox’s profit margins collapsed to just 3% this fiscal year, noting that organic revenue has dropped over the last five years excluding the impact of Microsoft's $75 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard in 2023. Sharma declared that the downward trajectory "cannot continue" amid stagnant global console spending and escalating manufacturing costs. To counter the financial slump, Sharma is executing a dual-pronged strategy of aggressive cost-cutting and targeted blockbusting spending. The Information reported that Sharma is preparing significant layoffs and budget reductions across Xbox’s less-popular game studios. However, those savings will be funneled directly back into the division's most lucrative and recognizable intellectual properties, keeping the overall game development budget relatively flat year over year. Microsoft’s top leadership has tentatively approved an increased game-development budget for the upcoming fiscal year starting in July, specifically targeted at fast-tracking new mainline entries for "industry-defining franchises" that Sharma claims have historically lacked adequate funding. A primary focus of the investment surge includes accelerating development timelines for core franchises like Halo, Fallout, and The Elder Scrolls. The move attempts to address prolonged gaps in major releases; The Elder Scrolls and Fallout have not seen new mainline titles debut since 2011 and 2014, respectively, while the flagship Halo franchise has lacked a major release since 2021. Sharma has informed deputies that the division must publish new Halo games on a significantly faster timeline. Additional resources are also expected to be allocated to Minecraft to help the title recover ground lost to competitors like Roblox in daily active user metrics. "Asha was put in there either to get rid of the business or fix it, and her actions so far show she's trying to fix it," Wedbush Securities Managing Director Michael Pachter told The Information, noting that the upcoming layoffs and accelerated production timelines represent necessary steps to rein in bloated operational costs. Robinhood Markets Inc (HOOD) experienced significant platform strain on Friday as retail investors flooded the app to trade shares of SpaceX following its record-breaking initial public offering. The brokerage’s official help account posted on X that the platform saw “record-breaking traffic today,” resulting in “latency and intermittent issues” for some customers. Essential systems later recovered, the company said, with teams continuing to monitor performance. Shares of the company, however, gained 1% at the time of writing. The issues coincided with the Nasdaq debut of SpaceX (SPCX), the largest IPO in U.S. history. The company priced 555.6 million shares at $135 each, raising around $75 billion and valuing the business at roughly $1.77 trillion at the offering price. Downdetector showed a sharp spike in outage reports, at about 4,000 around midday Eastern Time, with users describing problems in placing, canceling or executing orders, particularly involving the newly listed SPCX shares. Complaints on social media included stuck stop-loss and limit orders, delayed executions and difficulty exiting positions during the volatile opening. Several users reported being unable to adjust risk-management tools or sell shares promptly, with some alleging financial losses tied to the disruptions. One trader posted that the outage prevented them from exiting a position, resulting in “thousands of dollars in losses.” Others described pending orders remaining unresolved for over an hour and an inability to modify stop orders on SPCX. Robinhood had been a prominent channel for retail participation in the IPO through its IPO Access program, amplifying the surge in activity once trading began. Despite the brokerage hiccups, SPCX opened at approximately $150 — an 11% premium to the IPO price — and climbed as much as 30% higher in early trading, briefly pushing the company’s market capitalization above $2.2 trillion. Shares of Enliven Therapeutics (ELVN) jumped 12% on Friday, on track to close its fourth consecutive day in the green, after the company announced that its experimental drug ELVN-001 showed encouraging results in patients with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), a type of blood cancer, in an updated Phase 1 study. The stock has risen about 33% this week and is on track to post its best week since last March if gains hold. As of March 2026, the drug produced meaningful responses in heavily pretreated patients, many of whom had already tried multiple existing therapies, the company said on Thursday. In one key group receiving an 80 mg daily dose, 48% of patients achieved a major molecular response — a standard measure of treatment success in CML — while 30% reached a deeper response. The drug was generally well tolerated, with most side effects being mild. However, 6% of patients discontinued the study due to adverse events, the company noted. The company also announced it has aligned with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on key elements of its planned late-stage trial. Enliven expects to begin the late-stage trial in the second half of 2026. Separately, Enliven priced an upsized public offering to raise capital for its programs. “The gross proceeds from the offering are expected to be around $400.0 million before deducting underwriting discounts and commissions and other offering expenses,” the company said in its pricing announcement. ELVN-001 is now the main focus of Enliven’s pipeline after the company decided last year to explore strategic alternatives for its other clinical program, ELVN-002. "We've got a pretty good idea of how to operate, just really large constellations, and do it safely now, right? We are the only operator that has any experience of that scale,” he said.
